name: Matter and Form
plain_explanation: Take a bronze sphere: the bronze is its 'matter,' the sphericity is its 'form.' More generally, whatever a thing is made of is its matter, and the shape or organizing structure that makes that stuff into 'a thing' at all is its form.
precise_definition: Aristotle's doctrine that concrete substances are compounds of matter (potentiality) and form (the principle that confers definiteness, unity, and actuality); form is said to be more real and more substantial than matter, and things become more 'actual' as they acquire more form.
why_it_mattered: It let Aristotle explain unity and individuation (why a lump of marble becomes 'a statue,' a 'thing') and, extended teleologically, why living organisms and even the cosmos develop toward ever-greater actuality and likeness to God.
historical_origin: Developed by Aristotle, in explicit reworking of Platonic metaphysics, chiefly in the Metaphysics.
examples: A bronze sphere: bronze is matter, sphericity is form
A calm sea: water is matter, smoothness is form
The soul as 'the form of the body,' giving it organic unity of purpose
objections: Zeller's criticism (quoted by Russell) that Aristotle 'had only half emancipated himself... from Plato's tendency to hypostatise ideas,' since forms, like Ideas, are treated as substantial and more real than matter

Russell's own objection: if two brass spheres are made, does each have its own particular sphericity (making form unknowable, contrary to Aristotle's system) or the same universal sphericity (making form indistinguishable from a Platonic Idea)? Aristotle has no clear escape from this dilemma
competing_positions: Plato's theory that Forms/Ideas exist independently of any matter that exemplifies them
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became central to medieval Scholastic metaphysics and to Aristotle's own doctrine of the soul as 'the form of the body.'
